summary: The note is a long encyclopedia-style overview of walking as a locomotion gait, covering how it differs from running, its speed and health benefits, evolutionary origins including bipedalism in hominins, and its many variants such as Nordic walking, racewalking and pedestrianism. It also covers biomechanics, leisure and tourism events, walkability and urban planning, walking robots, mathematical models, and walking in animals like horses, elephants, fish and insects. The text is truncated mid-section in the insect gait discussion.
one_line: An overview of walking as a gait, covering its biomechanics, health benefits, evolution, variants, leisure culture, urban walkability, robotics and animal locomotion.
key_facts: Walking is defined by an "inverted pendulum" gait in which the body vaults over the stiff limb or limbs with each step.
The average human walking speed at crosswalks is about 5.0 km/h, or about 1.4 m/s, or about 3.1 mph.
Champion racewalkers can average more than 14 km/h (8.7 mph) over a distance of 20 km (12 mi).
An average human child achieves independent walking ability at around 11 months old.

A 2023 study by the European Journal of Preventive Cardiology found that walking at least 2,337 steps a day reduced the risk of dying from cardiovascular diseases, and 3,967 steps a day reduced the risk of dying from any cause.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported that people with diabetes who walked for two or more hours a week lowered their all-cause mortality rate by 39 percent.
Footprints discovered on a former shore in Kenya suggest ancestors of modern humans were walking in ways very similar to the present activity as long as 3 million years ago.
Nordic walking has been estimated as producing up to a 46% increase in energy consumption compared to walking without poles.
The Vierdaagse (Four Day Event) in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, has taken place since 1909 and is the world's largest multi-day walking event, with over 40,000 taking part.
The Labor Day walk on Mackinac Bridge, Michigan, draws over 60,000 participants and is the largest single-day walking event.
Central Copenhagen was converted from car traffic into a pedestrian zone in 1962.
The first purpose-built pedestrian street in Europe is the Lijnbaan in Rotterdam, opened in 1953.
In 2009, Japanese roboticist Tomotaka Takahashi developed a robot named Ropid that can jump three inches off the ground and walk, run and jump.
Elephants use only two gaits on land, the walk and a faster gait similar to running, and can reach a top speed of 18 km/h (11 mph).
The walk is a four-beat gait that averages about 4 miles per hour (6.4 km/h) in horses.
